la:verb:pello.gloss: to push, drive, hurl, impel, propel; expel, banish, eject, thrust out
senses: to push, drive, hurl, impel, propel; expel, banish, eject, thrust out
to rout, put to flight, discomfit
la:verb:pello.html:
pello, pĕpŭli, pulsum, 3 (
pluperf. pulserat, ), v. a.
kindred with Gr. πάλλω, πέλω
, to beat, strike, knock any thing or at any thing; to push, drive, hurl, impel, propel.
Lit.
In gen. (mostly poet.; syn.: trudo, percutio): pueri pulsi,: pectora pellite tonsis, Enn. ap. Fest. s. v. tonsa, p. 356 Müll. (Ann. v. 235 Vahl.): terram pede,: ter pede terram (in the tripudium),: humum pedibus,: fores,; : impetu venientium pulsae fores,: spumat sale rate pulsum, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 378 Vahl.); cf.: unda pulsa remis, Fragm. ap. ; so, vada remis,: (arbor) ventis pulsa,.—
In partic.
To drive out or away, to thrust or turn out, expel, banish; esp. milit., to drive back, discomfit, rout the enemy (freq. and class.; syn.: fugo, elimino, deicio); constr. with abl., with ex, rarely with de; also with ab and abl. of the place from which one is repelled or driven back, but has not entered: cum viri boni lapidibus e foro pellerentur,; so, omnes ex Galliae finibus,; and: praesidium ex arce,: a foribus,: istum ab Hispaniā,: patriis ab agris Pellor,; cf. : aliquem a sacris,: possessores suis sedibus,: aliquem sedibus,: aliquem possessionibus,: aliquem civitate,: loco,: patria,: aliquem regno,; .—Of inanim. objects: aquam de agro,: tecta, quibus frigorum vis pelleretur,: placidam nives pectore aquam,; : calculos e corpore,.—Without indicating the place whence: qui armis perterritus, fugatus, pulsus est,: hostes pelluntur,; cf.: milites pulsi fugatique,: exsules tyrannorum injuriā pulsi,driven out, banished,: Athenienses Diagoram philosophum pepulerunt,ext.— With abl. of manner: pudendis Volneribus pulsus,; cf.: si fugisset vulneratus a tergo, etc., Serv. ad loc.—Specifying the place whither: miles pellitur foras,: in exsilium pulsus,.—
In milit. lang., to rout, put to flight, discomfit: exercitum ejus ab Helvetiis pulsum et sub jugum missum,: compluribus his proeliis pulsis,: Romanos pulsos superatosque,fin., etc.; 1, 52; ; ; .—
To strike, set in motion, impel: inpello, sagitta pulsa manu,.—
Of a musical instrument, to strike the chords, play: nervi pulsi,struck,: lyra pulsa manu,; cf.: classica pulsa,i. e. blown,.—
Trop.
In gen., to strike, touch, move, affect, impress, etc. (class.): totum corpus hominis et ejus omnis vultus omnesque voces, ut nervi in fidibus, ita sonant, ut a motu animi quoque sunt pulsae,; cf. of sound: Ille canit, pulsae referunt ad sidera valles,: sonat amnis, et Asia longe Pulsa palus,: quemadmodum visa nos pellerent,; cf.: visa enim ista cum acriter mentem sensumve pepulerunt,; : quod (dictum) cum animos hominum aurisque pepulisset,: species utilitatis pepulit eum,: fit saepe, ut pellantur animi vehementius,: nec habet ullum ictum, quo pellat animum,: nulla me ipsum privatim pepulit insignis injuria,: ipsum in Hispaniā juvenem nullius forma pepulerat captivae,: non mediocri curā Scipionis animum pepulit,: pulsusque residerat ardor,: longi sermonis initium pepulisti,you have struck the chord of a long discussion,.—
In partic.
Todrive out or away, to banish, expel: maestitiam ex animis,: procul a me dolorem,: pulsus Corde dolor,: glandt famem,; so, sitim,: frigoris vim tectis,: somnum,; Col. poët. 10, 69: Phoebeā morbos arte,: vino curas,: moram,: dolore pulsa est amentia,: turpia crimina a vobis,: umbras noctis,: sidera,: nubila,: tenebras,; 15, 651.—
To beat, conquer, overcome (very rare): si animus hominem pepulit, actum'st: animo servit, non sibi; Sin ipse animum pepulit, vivit, victor victorum cluet,: alicui pudicitiam,.

senses: the plain, especially in the Aeneid
la:noun:pelagus.html:
pĕlăgus, i (Gr. plur. pelagē, ; ), n., = πέλαγος,
the sea (poet. and in post-Aug. prose for Lat. mare): fervit aestu pelagus, Pac. ap. : pelagus remis petere coeperunt, Auct. B. Hisp. 40: in pelago,: pelagus tenuere rates, the open sea, the main.

: pelago Danaūm insidias Praecipitare,: pelago dare vela patenti,; : qui fragilem truci Commisit pelago ratem,: pelago terrāque pericula passus,: lustrare pelagus,; ; ; : saeviente pelago,: vortices pelagi,: nantes lubrico pelagi,: pelagus Ciliciae,.— Poet., a mass of water, like the sea: pelago premit arva sonanti,.—

Fig., for an immense mass or extent: quam pauca excepta verba ex pelago sermonis pulli minus trita afferant,the ocean of vulgar language,: Herodiani scriptorum pelagus,; cf. a sea of troubles, Shaksp.

la:noun:pellis.gloss: animal skin; pelt, fell, hide; leather
senses: animal skin; pelt, fell, hide; leather
a garment, article of clothing made of skin
a tent for soldiers (they were covered with skins)
a thin peelable film covering the outside of a sporocarp
la:noun:pellis.html:
pellis, is (
abl. sing. pelle; but pelli,; ), f.
Gr. πέλλα, πέλας, skin; cf. ἐρυσίπελας, ἐπιπολή, surface; also, πλατύς, and Lat. palam
, a skin, hide (of a beast), whether on the body or taken off; a felt, pelt, etc.
Lit., : inaurata arietis, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 285 Vahl.): rana rugosam inflavit pellem,; : nationes caprarum pellibus vestitae,; cf.: quam tu numquam vides nisi cum pelle caprinā,: pelles pro velis,: fulvique insternor pelle leonis,: pelles perficere,: pelles candidas conficere,: pecudes aureas habuisse pelles tradiderunt,.—Poet., of the human skin: frigida pellis Duraque,: ossa atque pellis tota est,; : pellis nostra,; id. Job, 10, 11; 19, 20: pellem habere Hercules fingitur, ut homines cultus antiqui admoneantur. Lugentes quoque diebus luctus in pellibus sunt, Paul. ex Müll.; cf.: deformem pro cute pellem aspice,.—Prov.: detrahere pellem, i. e. to pull off the mask which conceals a person's faults, : introrsum turpis, speciosus pelle decorā,with a showy outside,: cf. : in propriā pelle quiescere, to be content with one's own state or condition, (v. pellicula): caninam pellem rodere, said of lampooning a slanderer,: pellem pro pelle, et cuncta quae habet homo dabit pro animā suā,: si mutare potest Aethiops pellem suam,.—
Transf.
Leather: ruptā calceus alter Pelle patet,.—
A garment, article of clothing made of skin, ; cf. : pes in pelle natet,in the shoe,; .—
A tent for soldiers (because it was covered with skins); usually in the phrase sub pellibus, in the camp: ut non multum imperatori sub ipsis pellibus otii relinquatur,: sub pellibus milites contineri non possent,: (Caesar) sub pellibus hiemare constituit,; cf. : durare sub pellibus,; ; : pellium nomine,for covering shields,.—
Parchment: pellibus exiguis artatur Livius ingens,on little parchments,.—
A drum: pelles caedere,.

la:noun:pella.html:
Pella, ae, and Pellē, ēs, f., = Πέλλα,
a city of remote antiquity in Macedonia, the birthplace of Alexander the Great, now Alaklisi, or Apostolus, ; ; ; ; .— Hence,
Pellaeus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to Pella, Pellœan.
Lit.: unus Pellaeo juveni non sufficit orbis,i.e. for Alexander,; also: ductor,: tyrannus,: Pellaeus Eoum qui domuit Porum,: Pellaeo ponte Niphaten adstrinxit,: Pellaei proles vesana Philippi,.—
Transf.
Macedonian: gladius,: sarissae,: aula,. —
Alexandrian (because Alexander founded Alexandria, in Egypt): Pellaeae arces,: muri,: gula (because the Alexandrians were famous gourmands),.—
In a gen. sense, Egyptian: Pellaei gens fortunata Canopi,: puer,i.e. Ptolemy,; also: rex,; cf. diadema,: sceptra,: domus,the palace of the Ptolemies,.

la:other:Pelusium.html:
Pēlūsĭum, ii, n., = Πηλούσιον,
an Egyptian city at the eastern mouth of the Nile, the modern Castle of Tineh, ; ; ; .—Hence,
Pēlūsĭăcus, a, um, adj., Pelusiac: lens,: linum, Plin 19, 1, 2, § 14: ostium Nili,; : via, leading toPelusium, .—
Pēlū-sĭānus, a, um, adj., Pelusian: mala,.—
Pēlūsĭōta or Pēlūsĭō-tes, ae, m., a Pelusian: Pelusiotae caepe non edunt,.—Acc.: Pelusioten,, n. 7.—
Pēlūsĭus, a, um, adj., Pelusian: vada Pelusia,: linteum,: munera,.

pēlĭcātus (pelli-, paeli-), ūs, m.
paelex

la:verb:pellicio.html:
pellĭcĭo or perlĭcĭo, lexi, lectum, 3 (collat. form pellĭcĕo, ēre, P.; ib., prob. on account of the
perf. pellicuit, Liv. Andron. ap. ib.), v. a.
per-lacio
, to allure, entice, inveigle, decoy, coax, wheedle, etc.
Lit. (class.): pellexit, in fraudem induxit, Paul. ex Müll.; : is senem per epistolas Pellexit,: mulierem imbecilli consilii pellexit ad se,: animum adulescentis,: populum in servitutem,: qui Chaucos ad deditionem pellicerent,: militem donis, populum annonā, cunctos dulcedine otii pellexit,: Florus pellicere alam equitum, ut, etc.,: animas instabiles, Pet. 2, 14.—Poet.: nec poterat quemquam placidi pellacia ponti Subdola pellicere in fraudem ridentibus undis,; .—
Transf.: alienam segetem (alienas fruges, etc.), to draw away the fruits of another's land to one's own by incantations and magical arts, ; .—
Trop.: meā quidem sententiā multo majorem partem sententiarum sale tuo et lepore et politissimis facetiis pellexisti,have brought over to your side,.

la:noun:Peleus.html:
Pēleus, ĕi and ĕos (
gen. Peleos, ; acc. Pelea, ; voc. Peleu, ; ; abl. Peleo, ), m., = Πηλεύς, a king of Thessaly, son of Æacus, brother of Telamon, half-brother of Phocus, husband of Thetis, father of Achilles, and a sharer in the expedition of the Argonauts, ; ; sqq.; ; ; .— Hence,
Pēlēïus, a, um, adj., Peleian, poet. for Achillean: facta,: virgo, of Achilles (Briseis), . —
Pēlīdes, ae, m.
The son of Peleus, i. e. Achilles, ; : Pelidae currus,; ; ; : lites Inter Peliden et inter Atriden,; ; .—
Also, the son of Achilles: Neoptolemus,.

la:other:Peloponnesus.html:
Pĕlŏponnēsus, i, f., = Πελοπόννησος (the island of Pelops),
the Peloponnesus, the southern part of Greece, so named from Pelops, who settled there, the modern Morea, ; ; ; 8; 2, 7, 10; ; ; ; .—Prov.: nos juveni, ut rogas, suppeditabimus et Peloponnesum ipsam sustinebimus, i. e. will exert ourselves to the utmost, will try to make impossibilities possible (cf. the Greek proverb. Ἀρκαδίαν μʼ αἰτεῖς, μέγα μʼ αἰτεῖς), ; cf. .—Hence,
Pĕlŏponnensis, e, adj., Peloponnesian. —Subst.: Pĕlŏponnensēs, ĭum, m., the Peloponnesians (post-class.), (Jeep. Peloponnensii); ; .—
Pĕlŏponnēsĭăcus, a, um, adj., Peloponnesian: litus,: ora,: gentes,: bellum,; .—In plur.: Pĕ-lŏponnēsĭăci, ōrum, m., the Peloponnesians, .—
Pĕlŏponnēsĭus, a, um, adj., Peloponnesian: civitates,: bellum,; Thras. 1, 3: circa Peloponnesia tempora,about the time of the Peloponnesian war,.—Hence, Pĕlŏponnēsii, ōrum, m., the Peloponnesians, ; .
